## 1. Introduction & Dataset Overview

This project investigates structural brain aging and cognitive decline using the *Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS)* cross-sectional dataset. We load the dataset and remove the 20 repeat scans to ensure statistical independence across observations.

⁠ {r load-data}
file_path <- resolve_data_file("data/oasis_cross-sectional-5708aa0a98d82080.xlsx")
raw_data <- read_oasis_file(file_path)
oasis_df <- prepare_oasis_data(raw_data, keep_first_scan_only = TRUE)
cat("Total unique participants loaded:", nrow(oasis_df), "\n")
 ⁠

## 2. Interactive OASIS Data Explorer (Shiny Application)

To explore bivariate relationships and test separate group regression slopes interactively, run the chunk below in RStudio:

⁠ {r shiny-app, eval=FALSE}
source("add_shiny_app.R")
run_oasis_app(exclude_repeats = TRUE)
 ⁠

## 3. Statistical Analyses

We address three research questions:

•⁠  ⁠*RQ1:* Does normalized whole brain volume (nWBV) predict cognitive performance (MMSE) over and above age, education, socioeconomic status (SES) and sex? Hierarchical multiple regression with heteroscedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors.
•⁠  ⁠*RQ2:* Does nWBV differ across dementia severity groups (CDR 0, CDR 0.5, CDR ≥ 1)? Welch's one-way ANOVA with Games–Howell post hoc tests, a Kruskal–Wallis test as a robustness check, and an age- and sex-adjusted model.
•⁠  ⁠*RQ3:* Does age moderate the association between nWBV and MMSE? Moderated multiple regression with mean-centered predictors, covariates and HC3 standard errors, followed by simple slopes at the 25th, 50th and 75th age percentiles.

Assumptions (multicollinearity, heteroscedasticity, influential cases, equality of variances) are checked within each analysis. Running the chunk below performs all three analyses and prints the results and plots.

⁠ {r statistical-analyses}
source("statistical_analyses.R")
 ⁠

## 4. Results

*RQ1 – Brain volume and cognition.* nWBV alone explained 23.1% of the variance in MMSE, F(1, 214) = 58.32, p < .001. Adding age did not improve the model (Δ*R*² = .004, p = .272), adding education and SES did (Δ*R*² = .056, p < .001), and adding sex did not (Δ*R*² = .000, p = .883). The final model explained 29.1% of the variance (adjusted R² = .274). nWBV remained a significant positive predictor: holding the covariates constant, a 0.01-unit higher nWBV was associated with a 0.39-point higher MMSE score (95% CI [0.24, 0.54], p < .001, β = .55). None of the covariates was individually significant, although education was borderline (p = .052).

*RQ2 – Brain volume across dementia severity.* Mean nWBV differed strongly across CDR groups, Welch's F(2, 89.03) = 49.53, p < .001, η² = .26. Brain volume decreased step by step from no dementia (M = .769) to very mild dementia (M = .729) to mild/moderate dementia (M = .705), and all three pairwise Games–Howell comparisons were significant (all adjusted p ≤ .002). A Kruskal–Wallis test led to the same conclusion, and the group difference remained significant after adjusting for age and sex (robust F(2, 230) = 19.89, p < .001, partial η² = .18).

*RQ3 – Age as a moderator.* The nWBV × age interaction was not significant (b = −0.0035, 95% CI [−0.0110, 0.0039], p = .351). Simple slopes were similar at ages 66 (b = 0.42), 73 (b = 0.40) and 81 (b = 0.37), all p < .001. There is therefore no evidence that the brain volume–cognition association changes with age, although this does not show that it is identical at all ages.

*Summary.* Greater brain volume was consistently associated with better cognitive performance and lower dementia severity, and this association did not depend on age.

## 5. Limitations

•⁠  ⁠The data are cross-sectional and observational, so the results describe differences between people, not change within a person or causal effects of brain volume on cognition.
•⁠  ⁠MMSE has a ceiling of 30, which may weaken associations among cognitively healthy participants.
•⁠  ⁠The higher CDR groups are small (CDR ≥ 1 merged, n = 30), which limits the precision of those estimates.
•⁠  ⁠Heteroscedasticity was present in the regression models; HC3 robust standard errors were used to account for it.
